summary: Defines LoST, an XML-based protocol that maps a service identifier and a location, geodetic or civic, to service contact URIs. It can find the right Public Safety Answering Point for emergency calls. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: You tell the system where you are and what help you need, and it tells you who to call there. LoST is how a phone finds the right emergency center.

questions: how do emergency calls find the right psap
how does lost find the right psap
what is a service boundary in lost
subtitle: How a device asks "who handles this service where I am?" and gets back the right contact address, such as the local emergency call center.

tldr.problem: For some services, such as emergency calling, the right server depends on both the service and where the caller is, and it is the one with jurisdiction over that spot, not necessarily the nearest.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a service identifier (a service URN) and a civic or geodetic location in an XML query carried over HTTP or HTTPS. The LoST server maps it to one or more service URIs plus a service region and an expiry time that allow caching.
tldr.outcome: LoST gives location-based call routing a standard lookup, including for the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) of an emergency call. It has since been updated by RFC 6848, RFC 8917 and RFC 9036.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: HTTP POST, over HTTP or HTTPS

today: RFC 5222 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2008 and has been updated by RFC 6848, RFC 8917 and RFC 9036. Read those updates together with this document.

sections.title: Mapping a Location to a Service
sections.content:
Protocols such as NAPTR records and the Service Location Protocol can find servers that offer a service. For some services, though, the right instance depends on both the service and the geographic location of whoever needs it. Emergency telecommunications is the key example: the right Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) is the one with jurisdiction over the caller's location, which is not necessarily the closest one by network or by line of sight.

LoST, Location-to-Service Translation, maps a service identifier (a service URN) and location information to one or more service URIs, such as sip, xmpp and tel URIs. The initial focus is emergency services, but the RFC says it is likely applicable to others, such as the US "2-1-1" and "3-1-1" numbers.

Queries can carry civic or geodetic locations, can be resolved recursively or iteratively, and support caching. The RFC covers only the protocol between mapping client and mapping server; server discovery, data replication and the overall architecture are left to a separate document. Messages are carried in HTTP and HTTPS.
sections.eli5: The closest fire station is not always the one that covers your street. LoST helps a phone find the one that is really responsible for where you are.

sections.title: The Four Queries
sections.content:
LoST has four request types, each with a matching response:

  • <findService> returns contact URIs for a location and service. It can also ask for location validation and service numbers.
  • <getServiceBoundary> fetches a service boundary.
  • <listServices> asks a server which services it supports, mainly for diagnostics.
  • <listServicesByLocation> asks which services are available for a given place.

Clients may query at any time. Common triggers are start-up or attaching to a network, noticing that the location has moved outside the service region, a SIP message reaching a proxy that does location-based call routing, expiry of a cached mapping, and invoking the service itself.

A service-specific Best Current Practice document governs whether a client queries just before needing the service or relies on cached answers. As a guideline, URI schemes that cannot actually start a contact (the RFC names data, info, cid and tag) should be avoided.
sections.eli5: You can ask four things: who should I call here, what is the shape of the area they cover, what kinds of help do you know about, and what kinds of help exist at this place.

sections.title: Finding a LoST Server
sections.content:
A LoST server is identified by a U-NAPTR/DDDS application unique string, which is a DNS name such as lostserver.example.com. The client uses U-NAPTR to turn that name into a URI saying which host and protocol to use. Only the HTTP and HTTPS URL schemes are defined here, and the HTTPS URL can be listed with a lower preference number than the HTTP one so that it is tried first.

How a client learns the server's name is outside this RFC. The RFC mentions SIP configuration and DHCP as examples, and a companion document, RFC 5223, covers discovery over DHCP.
sections.eli5: The phone looks up the helper's name in a phone book (DNS) and gets back the address and the way to talk to it, with the safer way listed first.

sections.title: The Mapping Element
sections.content:
The <mapping> element is the core data element. It describes a service region and the service URLs that go with it.

  • source, sourceId and lastUpdated are all REQUIRED. Together they identify one mapping record, are set by the authoritative source and never changed when served from a cache. A receiver may replace a mapping with one that has the same source and sourceId and a more recent lastUpdated.
  • expires is REQUIRED and gives the time the mapping becomes invalid. It may instead be NO-CACHE or NO-EXPIRATION. If a server has to return an expired mapping, the client MUST check expires and local policy decides whether to use it.
  • <displayName> gives a human-readable name, tagged with a language.
  • <service> is mandatory. If the requested service does not exist for the location, the server either returns a serviceNotImplemented error or supplies an alternative service URN.
  • <serviceBoundary> gives the region by value, or <serviceBoundaryReference> gives it by reference. The reference is a random token with at least 128 bits of entropy, and a new one MUST be chosen when the boundary changes.
  • <serviceNumber> holds digits, the star key and the hash key, for a 12-key dial pad.
  • <uri> elements hold absolute URLs, in no significant order, with each scheme at most once.

Every request that allows recursion carries a <path> of <via> elements naming each server in order, to prevent loops and allow tracing. Each <location> has an id, and the response returns it in <locationUsed> so the client knows which location the server used.
sections.eli5: An answer is like a card that says who to call, which area the card is good for, who wrote it, and when it goes out of date.

sections.title: Asking and Answering With findService
sections.content:
<findService> is the core of LoST. The request carries one or more <location> elements, at most one per location profile and in order of preference, and a <service> URN such as urn:service:sos.police. The server uses the first location whose profile it understands. In the RFC's geodetic example, a point at 37.775 -122.422 maps to a police department with two URIs, a boundary polygon, and service number 911. The civic example uses a Munich address and returns number 110.

Two attributes shape the request. recursive defaults to false: when true, the server queries other servers on the client's behalf, and when false it MUST NOT recurse and may instead redirect the client to the next server. serviceBoundary asks for the boundary value or a reference, though the server decides. A reference is fetched later with <getServiceBoundary>, sent to the authoritative server without recursion. Only <findService> and <listServicesByLocation> can be recursive.

Setting validateLocation to true asks for civic address validation. The server SHOULD answer with a <locationValidation> element listing address parts that are <valid>, <invalid> or <unchecked>. In the RFC's example, the country and state, city and street parts were valid, the postal code was invalid, and the house number was unchecked.
sections.eli5: You hand over your spot and the kind of help you want. The helper either answers or asks a friend and passes the answer back, and it can also tell you which parts of your address look wrong.

sections.title: Location Profiles
sections.content:
Location can be written in many ways, which causes interoperability problems. LoST therefore defines two mandatory-to-implement location profiles: geodetic-2d (points, polygons, circles, ellipses and arc bands from the GEOPRIV PIDF-LO work) and civic (a civic address element). New profiles need Standards Action.

The rules that keep clients and servers compatible include:

  • A client that sends any non-baseline profile MUST also send one of the baseline profiles in the same request.
  • A client MUST NOT mix baseline profiles. If it has both geodetic and civic information, it MUST send separate requests.
  • Only one instance of each profile per query, and servers MUST implement all profiles in the document.
  • A server uses the first profile it understands, and the <serviceBoundary> in the response states the profile it used.

When a client sends a shape rather than a point, it accepts results for any part of it. A server MAY return several mappings, but is not required to return all of them, which protects it from queries that span very many service boundaries. An authoritative server whose coverage overlaps the query MUST return either a mapping that intersects the query area or a redirect to a server with a subset of its coverage. In emergency use, the PSAP contacted may need to forward the call to a neighbor, which the RFC calls an expected part of the system.
sections.eli5: People can describe where they are as a street address or as map coordinates. LoST makes sure both sides always know at least one of those two ways, so they can understand each other.

sections.title: Errors, Warnings, Redirects and Transport
sections.content:
A server returns an <errors> element when no useful response is possible, and a <warnings> element inside another response when it could answer only in part. Each carries a human-readable message, a language tag, and a source naming the server that produced it. Warnings defined are locationValidationUnavailable, serviceSubstitution (for example, answering with urn:service:sos where sub-services like police are not used) and defaultMappingReturned (for example, a nearby PSAP).

A <redirect> names the next server in its target attribute, which the client SHOULD contact. The same location and service SHOULD NOT be sent to the redirecting server before the time given in the expires value of the answer it points to.

For transport, LoST is defined over HTTP and HTTP-over-TLS using the POST method, with media type application/lost+xml. The request MUST use the Cache-Control directive no-cache. All LoST responses, including errors and warnings, travel in 2xx HTTP responses, usually 200. 3xx, 4xx and 5xx responses mean the HTTP request itself failed and contain no LoST XML. LoST clients and servers MUST understand UTF-8 and UTF-16 XML and MUST NOT use other encodings.
sections.eli5: If the helper cannot answer, it says why. If it can only half answer, it adds a note. If someone else is better placed, it tells you to ask them instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several threats. An attacker with service contact URIs could try to disrupt those services, and one who blocks lookups can make services unreachable. An eavesdropper may infer that an emergency exists and its nature, and possibly attack the caller physically.

TLS MUST be implemented and SHOULD be used, and use is RECOMMENDED both for client queries and for queries among servers, which helps prevent cache poisoning. Checking the server's identity is also RECOMMENDED. The host name checked against the certificate is the host name in the URI, not the DNS name fed into NAPTR resolution, because many inputs would resolve to one emergency-authority server.

That choice leaves DNS-based attacks possible, since an attacker may alter NAPTR records. DNSSEC can protect against this, but the RFC notes it is incompletely deployed. Deployments that cannot rely on DNSSEC can configure LoST server URIs directly. Servers generally need not authenticate clients, but if they do, HTTP basic or digest authentication MAY be used, and basic authentication SHOULD only be used with TLS. Non-emergency uses may face different threats, so new contexts need their own analysis.
sections.eli5: Bad people might want to know where help is, block you from finding it, or lie to your phone. So the chat is locked with TLS and the phone checks it is talking to the real helper.
